contenido: 1. The Church professes its faith in the Holy Spirit who is "Lord and giver of life." This is what the Symbol of Faith professes, called Nicene-Constantinopolitan after the name of the two Councils âNicea ( [+[0]+] ) and Constantinople ( [+[1]+] )â, in which it was formulated or promulgated. They also add that the Holy Spirit "spoke through the prophets." They are words that the Church receives from the very source of its faith, Jesus Christ. In fact, according to the Gospel of John, the Holy Spirit is given to us with the new life, as Jesus announces and promises on the great day of the Feast of Tabernacles: « "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him who believes in me drink", as the Scripture says: Rivers of living water will flow from his bosom. by Jesus in his conversation with the Samaritan woman, when he speaks of a "fountain of water springing up for eternal life,"3 and in his conversation with Nicodemus, when he announces the need for a new birth "of water and of the Spirit" to "enter the Kingdom of God."4

2. This faith, professed uninterruptedly by the Church, must always be strengthened and deepened in the conscience of the People of God. Over the last century this has happened several times; from Leo XIII, who published the Encyclical Divinum illud munus ( [+[0]+] ) dedicated entirely to the Holy Spirit, through Pius deepening of the doctrine on the Holy Spirit, as Paul VI emphasized: "Christology and especially the ecclesiology of the Council must be succeeded by a new study and a new cult of the Holy Spirit, precisely as a necessary complement to the conciliar doctrine."6

3. When the time for Jesus to leave this world was imminent, he announced to the apostles "another Paraclete."16 The Evangelist John, who was present, writes that Jesus, during the Passover Supper prior to the day of his passion and death, addressed them with these words: "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son... and I will ask the Father and he will give you another Paraclete to be with you to always, the Spirit of truth."17

4. Shortly after the aforementioned announcement, Jesus adds: "But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and will remind you of everything I have said."19 The Holy Spirit will be the Comforter of the apostles and the Church, always present among them - although invisible - as teacher of the same Good News that Christ announced. The words "teach" and "remember" mean not only that the Spirit, in his own way, will continue to inspire the preaching of the Gospel of salvation, but will also help to understand the just meaning of the content of Christ's message, ensuring its continuity and identity of understanding in the midst of changing conditions and circumstances. The Holy Spirit, then, will ensure that the same truth that the apostles heard from their Master always endures in the Church.

5. The apostles, when transmitting the Good News, will be particularly united to the Holy Spirit. Thus Jesus continues speaking: «When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me. But you will also bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. "20

6. This is also deduced from the deep correlation of content and intention with the aforementioned announcement and promise, which is found in the successive words of John's text: «I could still say much to you, but now you cannot bear it. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into the complete truth; for he will not speak on his own, but he will speak what he hears, and he will announce to you what is to come. "23

7. Between the Holy Spirit and Christ, therefore, there subsists in the economy of salvation an intimate relationship through which the Spirit acts in the history of man as "another Paraclete", permanently ensuring the transmission and irradiation of the Good News revealed by Jesus of Nazareth. For this reason, the glory of Christ shines in the Holy Spirit-Paraclete, who in the mystery and activity of the Church incessantly continues the historical presence of the Redeemer on earth and his saving work, as witnessed by the following words of John: "He will give me glory, because he will receive what is mine and will communicate it to you."25 With these words everything that the previous statements have said is confirmed once again. «He will teach..., he will remember..., he will bear witness.» The supreme and complete self-revelation of God, which has been realized in Christ, witnessed by the preaching of the Apostles, continues to be manifested in the Church through the mission of the invisible Paraclete, the Spirit of truth. How closely this mission is related to the mission of Christ and how fully it is based on itself, consolidating and developing its salvific fruits in history, is expressed with the verb "receive": "he will receive of what is mine and will communicate it to you." Jesus, to explain the word "receive", clearly highlighting the divine and Trinitarian unity of the source, adds: "Everything the Father has is mine. That is why I have told you: He will receive what is mine and will communicate it to you. "26 By taking what is "mine", for this very reason he will receive "what is the Father's."

8. A characteristic of the Johannine text is that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are clearly called Persons; The first is different from the second and the third, and these are also different from each other. Jesus speaks of the Spirit Paraclete using the personal pronoun "he" several times; and at the same time, throughout the farewell speech, he discovers the ties that mutually unite the Father, the Son and the Paraclete. Therefore, "the Spirit... proceeds from the Father" 28 and the Father will "give" the Spirit.29 The Father will "send" the Spirit in the name of the Son, 30 the Spirit will "bear witness" to the Son.31 The Son asks the Father to send the Paraclete Spirit,32 but he further affirms and promises, in connection with his "departure" through the Cross: "If I go, I will send him to you."33 Thus, the Father sends the Holy Spirit with the power of his fatherhood, equally who has sent the Son,34 and at the same time sends him with the power of the redemption accomplished by Christ; In this sense the Holy Spirit is also sent by the Son: "I will send him to you."

9. Thus, in the farewell Easter discourse we reach, one might say, the culmination of the Trinitarian revelation. At the same time, we find ourselves before definitive events and supreme words, which in the end will be translated into the great missionary mandate addressed to the apostles and, through them, to the Church: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations," a mandate that contains, in a certain way, the Trinitarian formula of baptism: "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."35 This formula reflects the intimate mystery of God and of his divine life, which is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, divine unity of the Trinity. This discourse can be read as a special preparation for this Trinitarian formula, which expresses the life-giving force of the Sacrament that brings about participation in the life of the triune God, because it gives man sanctifying grace as a supernatural gift. Through it he is called and made "capable" of participating in the inscrutable life of God.

10. God, in his intimate life, "is love",36 essential love, common to the three divine Persons. THE Holy Spirit is personal love as the Spirit of the Father and the Son. For this reason he "probes to the depths of God",37 as uncreated Love-gift. It can be said that in the Holy Spirit the intimate life of the triune God becomes entirely a gift, an exchange of reciprocal love between the divine Persons, and that through the Holy Spirit God "exists" as a gift. The Holy Spirit is therefore the personal expression of this donation, of this being-love.38 He is Person-love. It is Person-gift. We have here an unfathomable richness of reality and an ineffable deepening of the concept of person in God, which we only know through Revelation.

11. Christ's farewell speech during the Passover Supper refers particularly to this "giving" and "giving" of the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel of John we discover the deepest "logic" of the saving mystery contained in the eternal plan of God as an expansion of the ineffable communion of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. It is the divine "logic", which from the mystery of the Trinity leads to the mystery of the Redemption of the world through Jesus Christ. The Redemption accomplished by the Son in the scope of man's earthly history â€“ accomplished by his "departure" through the Cross and Resurrection â€“ is at the same time, in all its saving power, transmitted to the Holy Spirit: who "will receive of mine."40 The words of the Johannine text indicate that, according to the divine plan, the "departure" of Christ is an indispensable condition of the "sending" and coming of the Holy Spirit, they indicate that then begins the new salvific communication by the Holy Spirit.

12. It is a new beginning in relation to the first, "original beginning of God's saving gift" that is identified with the mystery of creation. Thus we already read in the first pages of the book of Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth... and the Spirit of God ( [+[0]+] ) hovered above the waters."41 This biblical concept of creation involves not only the call of the very being of the cosmos into existence, that is, the giving of existence, but also the presence of the Spirit of God in creation, that is, the beginning of God's saving communication to the things he creates. Which is valid above all for man, who has been created in the image and likeness of God: "Let us make the human being in our image, in our likeness."42 "Let us make", can the plural, which the Creator uses here speaking of himself, already suggest in some way the Trinitarian mystery, the presence of the Trinity in the work of man's creation? The Christian reader, who already knows the revelation of this mystery, can also discover its reflection in these words. In any case, the context allows us to see in the creation of man the first beginning of God's saving gift to the extent of his "image and likeness", which he has granted to man.

13. It seems, then, that the words spoken by Jesus in the farewell speech must also be read with reference to that "beginning" so distant, but fundamental, that we know from Genesis. «If I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send it to you. Christ, describing his "departure" as a condition of the "coming" of the Paraclete, unites the new beginning of God's saving communication by the Holy Spirit with the mystery of Redemption. This is a new beginning, above all because between the first beginning and the entire history of man, “beginning with the original fall,” sin has intervened, which is contrary to the presence of the Spirit of God in creation and is, above all, contrary to the saving communication of God to man. Saint Paul writes that, precisely because of sin, "creation... was subjected to vanity... groaning to this day and suffering in travail" and "longing for the revelation of the children of God."43

14. That is why Jesus Christ says in the Cenacle: "It is better for you that I go away"; «If I leave, I will send it to you».44 The «departure» of Christ through the Cross has the force of Redemption; and this also means a new presence of the Spirit of God in creation: the new beginning of the communication of God to man by the Holy Spirit. « The proof that you are children is that God has sent into our hearts the Spirit of his Son who cries: Abba Father! », writes the apostle Paul in the Letter to the Galatians.45 The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, as the words of the farewell speech in the Upper Room attest. It is, at the same time, the Spirit of the Son: it is the Spirit of Jesus Christ, as the apostles and especially Paul of Tarsus will attest.46 With the sending of this Spirit "into our hearts" what "creation deeply desires" begins to be fulfilled, as we read in the Letter to the Romans.

15. The mission of the Messiah, who received the fullness of the Holy Spirit for the chosen People of God and for all humanity, is thus completely realized. «Messiah» literally means «Christ», that is, «anointed one»; and in salvation history it means "anointed with the Holy Spirit." This was the prophetic tradition of the Old Testament. Following her, Simon Peter will say in Cornelius' house: «You know what happened in all Judea... after John preached the baptism; as God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power.”50

16. The Messiah is precisely this way. In the Old Covenant the anointing was an external symbol of the gift of the Spirit. The Messiah ( [+[0]+] ) is the only great Anointed One by God Himself. He is the Anointed One in the sense that he possesses the fullness of the Spirit of God. He himself will also be the mediator when granting this Spirit to all the People. In fact, the Prophet says in these words:

contenido: 17. It is important to clearly emphasize here that the "Spirit of the Lord", which "rests" on the future Messiah, is above all a gift from God to the person of that Servant of the Lord. But this is not an isolated and independent person, because he acts by the will of the Lord by virtue of his decision or option. Although in the light of the texts of Isaiah the salvific action of the Messiah, Servant of the Lord, contains within itself the action of the Spirit that is manifested through himself, however in the Old Testament context the distinction of the divine subjects or persons, such as they subsist in the Trinitarian mystery and are later revealed in the New Testament, is not suggested. Both in Isaiah and in the rest of the Old Testament the personality of the Holy Spirit is totally "hidden": hidden in the revelation of the only God, as well as in the announcement of the future Messiah.

18. Jesus Christ will refer to this announcement, contained in the words of Isaiah, at the beginning of his messianic activity. This will happen in Nazareth itself, where he had spent thirty years of his life in the house of Joseph, the carpenter, with Mary, his Virgin Mother. When the opportunity arose to speak in the Synagogue, he opened the book of Isaiah and found the passage in which it was written: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me." Holy as a gift from God himself, he who possesses the fullness of this Spirit, he who marks the "new beginning" of the gift that God makes to humanity with the Spirit.

19. Although in Nazareth, his homeland, Jesus is not welcomed as the Messiah, however, at the beginning of his public activity, his messianic mission by the Holy Spirit is revealed to the people by John the Baptist. This, son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, announces in the Jordan the coming of the Messiah and administers the baptism of repentance. He says in this regard: «I baptize you with water; But he who is stronger than me is coming, and I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”65

20. The theophany of Jordan illuminates only fleetingly the mystery of Jesus of Nazareth whose entire activity will develop under the living presence of the Holy Spirit.70 This mystery would have been manifested by Jesus himself and gradually confirmed through everything he "did and taught."71 In line with this teaching and the messianic signs that Jesus made before reaching the farewell speech in the Cenacle, we find some events and words that constitute particularly important moments of this progressive revelation. Thus the evangelist Luke, who has already presented Jesus "filled with the Holy Spirit" and "led by the Spirit in the desert",72 lets us know that, after the return of the seventy-two disciples from the mission entrusted to them by the Master,73 while full of joy they narrated the fruits of their work, "at that moment, Jesus was filled with joy in the Holy Spirit, and said: "I bless you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise. and intelligent, and you have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for such has been your good pleasure."74 Jesus rejoices in divine paternity, he rejoices because it has been possible for him to reveal this paternity; Finally, he rejoices in the special irradiation of this divine paternity on the "little ones." And the evangelist describes all this as "joy in the Holy Spirit."

21. What during the Jordan theophany came in a certain way "from outside", from above here comes "from within", that is, from the depth of what Jesus is. It is another revelation of the Father and the Son, united in the Holy Spirit. Jesus speaks only of the fatherhood of God and his own sonship; It does not speak directly of the Spirit who is love and, therefore, union of the Father and the Son. However, what he says about the Father and about himself as the Son springs from the fullness of the Spirit that is in him and that pours out into his heart, penetrates his very "I", deeply inspires and vivifies his action. Hence that "rejoice in the Holy Spirit." The union of Christ with the Holy Spirit, of which he is perfectly aware, is expressed in that "joy", which in a certain way makes its arcane source "perceptible". Thus there is a particular manifestation and exaltation, which is proper to the Son of Man, of Christ-Messiah, whose humanity belongs to the person of the Son of God, substantially one with the Holy Spirit in divinity.

22. Thanks to his narration, Luke brings us closer to the truth contained in the Cenacle speech. Jesus of Nazareth, "elevated" by the Holy Spirit, during this discourse-colloquium, manifests himself as the one who "brings" the Spirit, as the one who must take it and "give" it to the apostles and the Church at the cost of his "departure" through the cross.

23. We find ourselves on the threshold of Easter events. The new and definitive revelation of the Holy Spirit as a Person, which is the gift, takes place precisely at this moment. The Easter events – passion, death and resurrection of Christ – are also the time of the new coming of the Holy Spirit, as Paraclete and Spirit of truth. They are the time of the "new beginning" of the communication of the triune God to humanity in the Holy Spirit, through the work of Christ the Redeemer. This new beginning is the redemption of the world: "God so loved the world that he gave his only Son."81 Already in the "giving" of the Son, in this gift of the Son, the deepest essence of God is expressed, which, as Love, is the inexhaustible source of this gift. In the gift made by the Son, the revelation and gift of eternal love are completed: the Holy Spirit, who in the inscrutable depth of divinity is a Person-gift, by the work of the Son, that is, through the paschal mystery, is given in a new way to the apostles and the Church and, through them, to humanity and the entire world.

24. The definitive expression of this mystery takes place on the day of the Resurrection. This day, Jesus of Nazareth, "born of the lineage of David," as the apostle Paul writes, is "established as the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by his resurrection from the dead."82 It can be said, therefore, that the messianic "elevation" of Christ by the Holy Spirit reaches its culmination in the Resurrection, in which he is also revealed as the Son of God, "full of power." And this power, whose sources spring from the inscrutable Trinitarian communion, is manifested above all in the fact that the risen Christ, if on the one hand he fulfills the promise of God already expressed by the mouth of the Prophet: "I will give you a new heart, I will put in you a new spirit, ... my spirit",83 on the other he fulfills his same promise made to the apostles with the words: If I go away, I will send him to you.84 It is he: the Spirit of truth, the Paraclete sent by the resurrected Christ to transform us into his resurrected image.85

25. « Once the work that the Father entrusted the Son to carry out on earth was completed ( [+[0]+] ), the Holy Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost in order to sanctify the Church indefinitely and so that in this way the faithful have access to the Father through Christ in the same Spirit ( [+[1]+] ). He is the Spirit of life or the fountain of water that springs up to eternal life ([+[2]+]), through whom the Father gives life to men, dead in sin, until he resurrects their mortal bodies in Christ ([+[3]+])."92

26. The passages cited by the conciliar Constitution Lumen gentium indicate to us that, with the coming of the Holy Spirit, the era of the Church began. They also tell us that this era, the era of the Church, endures. It lasts through centuries and generations. In our century in which humanity is approaching the end of the second millennium after Christ, this "age of the Church" has been manifested in a special way through the Second Vatican Council, as the council of our century. In fact, it is known that this has been especially an "ecclesiological" council, a council on the subject of the Church. At the same time, the teaching of this council is essentially "pneumatological", permeated by the truth about the Holy Spirit, as the soul of the Church. We can say that the Second Vatican Council in its rich magisterium properly contains everything "that the Spirit says to the Churches" 97 in the present phase of the history of salvation.

27. When Jesus, during the Cenacle speech, announces the coming of the Holy Spirit "at the cost" of his departure and promises: "If I go, I will send him to you," in precisely the same context he adds: "And when he comes, he will convince the world in regard to sin, in regard to justice, and in regard to judgment."102 The same Paraclete and Spirit of truth, "who has been promised as the one who will "teach" and " will remember", that "will bear witness", that "will guide to the complete truth"â, with the words quoted now he is announced as the one who "will convince the world regarding sin, regarding justice and regarding judgment."

28. We now want to concentrate our attention mainly on this mission of the Holy Spirit, which consists of "convicting the world about sin", but at the same time respecting the context of Jesus' words in the Cenacle. The Holy Spirit, who receives from the Son the work of the Redemption of the world, receives with it the task of the savior "to convince regarding sin." This convincing constantly refers to "justice", that is, to definitive salvation in God, to the fulfillment of the economy that has as its center the crucified and glorified Christ. And this saving economy of God, in a certain way, removes man from "judgment, that is, condemnation," with which the sin of Satan, "Prince of this world," has been punished, who by reason of his sin has become "dominator of this dark world" 106 and here, through this reference to "judgment," broad horizons are opened for the understanding of "sin" as well as "justice." The Holy Spirit, by showing in the framework of the Cross of Christ "sin" in the economy of salvation ([+[0]+]), makes it understood that his mission is to "convince" also with regard to sin that has already been definitively judged ([+[1]+]).

29. All the words, spoken by the Redeemer in the Cenacle on the eve of his passion, are inscribed in the era of the Church: above all, those said about the Holy Spirit as Paraclete and Spirit of truth. These are inscribed in it in an always new way throughout each generation and each era. This has been confirmed, with respect to our century, by all the teachings of the Second Vatican Council, especially in the Pastoral Constitution "Gaudium et spes." Many passages in this document clearly indicate that the Council, opening itself to the light of the Spirit of truth, presents itself as the authentic repository of the announcements and promises made by Christ to the apostles and the Church in the farewell speech; in particular, of the announcement, according to which the Holy Spirit must "convince the world regarding sin, regarding justice and regarding judgment."

30. On the day of Pentecost the announcements of Christ in the farewell speech and, in particular, the announcement we are dealing with found their most exact and direct confirmation: "The Paraclete... will convince the world regarding sin." That day, on the apostles gathered in prayer together with Mary, Mother of Jesus, the promised Holy Spirit descended, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit allowed them to express themselves",109 "in this way leading the dispersed races back to unity, offering to the Father the first fruits of all nations."110

31. Since this initial testimony of Pentecost, the action of the Spirit of truth, which "convicts the world regarding sin" of the rejection of Christ, is inseparably linked to the testimony of the paschal mystery: mystery of the Crucified and Risen. In this connection the same "convince regarding sin" manifests its own salvific dimension. In effect, it is a "conviction" whose purpose is not the mere accusation of the world, much less its condemnation. Jesus Christ has not come into the world to judge and condemn it, but to save it.114 This is already underlined in this first speech when Peter exclaims: "Let all the house of Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you have crucified, Lord and Christ."115 And then, when those present ask Peter and the other apostles: "What shall we do, brothers?" » He answers them: « Convert and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. "116

32. However, no one can "convince the world", man and human conscience of this ineffable truth, except the Spirit of truth. He is the Spirit who "probes the depths of God."121 Faced with the mystery of sin, "the depths of God" must be completely plumbed. It is not enough to probe the human conscience, as the intimate mystery of man, but one must penetrate the intimate mystery of God, into those "depths of God" that are summarized in the synthesis: to the Father, in the Son, through the Holy Spirit. It is precisely the Holy Spirit who "probes" them and draws from them God's response to man's sin. With this response the procedure of "convincing regarding sin" is completed, as evidenced by the event of Pentecost.

33. It is the dimension of sin that we find in the testimony of the beginning, collected in the Book of Genesis. 125 It is the sin that, according to the revealed word of God, constitutes the beginning and the root of all others. We are faced with the original reality of sin in the history of man and, at the same time, in the economy of salvation as a whole. It can be said that in this sin the mystery of impiety begins, but that this is also the sin, in respect of which the redemptive power of the mystery of piety becomes particularly transparent and effective. This is expressed by Saint Paul, when he contrasts the “disobedience” of the first Adam with the “obedience” of Christ, the second Adam: “Obedience unto death.”126

34. The "spirit of God", which according to the biblical description of creation "flittered above the waters",130 indicates the same "Spirit that probes to the depths of God", probes the depths of the Father and the Word-Son in the mystery of creation. Not only is he the direct witness of their mutual love, from which creation derives, but he himself is this love. He himself, as love, is the eternal uncreated gift. In him is the source and the beginning of all gifts to creatures. The testimony of the principle, which we find in all revelation beginning with the Book of Genesis, is univocal in this regard. Creating means calling into existence from nothing; Therefore, creating means giving existence. And if the visible world is created for man, therefore the world is given to man.131 And at the same time, man himself in his own humanity receives as a gift a special "image and likeness" of God. This means not only rationality and freedom as constitutive properties of human nature, but also, from the beginning, the capacity for a personal relationship with God, as "I" and "you" and, consequently, the capacity for alliance that will take place with the saving communication of God to man. Within the framework of the "image and likeness" of God, "the gift of the Spirit" means, finally, a call to friendship, in which the transcendental "depths of God" are open, in a certain way, to the participation of man. The Second Vatican Council teaches: "Invisible God ([+[0]+]) moved by love, speaks to men as friends, deals with them ([+[1]+]) to invite them and receive them into his company."132

35. Therefore, the Spirit, who "searches everything, even to the depths of God," knows from the beginning "the inmost depths of man."133 Precisely for this reason only he can fully "convince regarding the sin" that occurred in the beginning, a sin that is the root of all others and the focus of man's sinfulness on earth, which is never quenched. The Spirit of truth knows the original reality of sin, caused in the will of man by the work of the "father of lies" - of him who is already "judged".134 THE Holy Spirit, therefore, convinces the world regarding sin in relation to this "judgment", but constantly guiding towards the "justice" that has been revealed to man together with the Cross of Christ, through "obedience unto death".135

36. According to the testimony of the principle, which we find in Scripture and Tradition, after the first ( [+[0]+] ) description of Genesis, sin in its original form is understood as "disobedience", which means simply and directly transgression of a prohibition placed by God.136 But in view of the entire context it is also evident that the roots of this disobedience must be sought deeply in the entire real situation of man. Called into existence, the human being “man or woman” is a creature. The "image of God", which consists of rationality and freedom, demonstrates the greatness and dignity of the human subject, who is a person. But this personal subject is also a creature: in its existence and essence it depends on the Creator. According to Genesis, "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil" was to express and constantly remind man of the insurmountable "limit" for a created being. In this sense, God's prohibition must be understood: the Creator prohibits man and woman from eating the fruits of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The words of instigation, that is, of temptation, as formulated in the sacred text, induce you to transgress this prohibition, that is, to exceed that "limit": "the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil."137

contenido: 37. According to the testimony of the beginning, God in creation has revealed himself as omnipotence which is love. At the same time, it has revealed to man that, as the "image and likeness" of his creator, he is called to participate in truth and love. This participation means a life in union with God, which is "eternal life."138 But man, under the influence of the "father of lies," has separated himself from this participation. To what extent? Certainly not to the measure of the sin of a pure spirit, to the measure of Satan's sin. The human spirit is incapable of reaching such a measure.139 In the same description of Genesis it is easy to point out the difference in degree between "the breath of evil" of the one who is a sinner ([+[0]+]) from the beginning 140 and who is already "judged" 141 and the evil of man's disobedience. This disobedience, however, also means turning one's back on God and, in a certain way, closing human freedom from him. It also means a certain opening of this freedom "of knowledge and human will" towards him who is the "father of lies." This act of responsible choice is not only a "disobedience", but also carries with it a certain adherence to the motive contained in the first instigation to sin and constantly renewed throughout the history of man on earth: "God knows very well that on the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." Here we find ourselves at the very center of what could be called the "anti-Word", that is, the "anti-truth". In effect, the truth of man is falsified: who man is and what are the insurmountable limits of his being and his freedom. This "anti-truth" is possible, because at the same time the truth about who God is is completely falsified. God the Creator is placed in a state of suspicion, even more so in a state of accusation before the conscience of the creature. For the first time in the history of man, the perverse "genius of suspicion" appears. This tries to "falsify" the Good itself, the absolute Good, which in the work of creation has manifested itself precisely as the good that gives in an ineffable way: as bonum diffusivum sui, as creative love. Who can fully "convince regarding sin", that is, of this motivation for man's original disobedience, except he who alone is the gift and source of all gifts, but the Spirit who "probes the depths of God" and is the love of the Father and the Son?

contenido: 38. For, despite all the testimony of creation and the saving economy inherent in it, the spirit of darkness 142 is capable of showing God as the enemy of the creature itself and, above all, as the enemy of man, as a source of danger and threat to man. In this way Satan grafts into the spirit of man the germ of opposition to him who "from the beginning" must be considered as man's enemy and not as Father. Man is challenged to become God's adversary.

39. THE Spirit, who probes the depths of God, has been called by Jesus in the speech of the Cenacle the Paraclete. In fact, from the beginning "he is invoked" 145 to "convince the world regarding sin." It is invoked definitively through the Cross of Christ. Convincing regarding sin means demonstrating the evil contained in it. Which is equivalent to revealing the mystery of impiety. It is not possible to understand the evil of sin in all its painful reality without probing the depths of God. From the beginning the dark mystery of sin has manifested itself in the world with a clear reference to the Creator of human freedom. It has appeared as a voluntary act of the creature-man contrary to the will of God: the saving will of God; Furthermore, it has appeared as opposition to the truth, on the basis of the lie already definitively "judged": a lie that has placed creative and saving love itself in a state of accusation, in a state of permanent suspicion. Man has followed the "father of lies", placing himself against the Father of life and the Spirit of truth.

40. The redemptive value of Christ's sacrifice has been expressed in very significant words by the author of the Letter to the Hebrews, who, after having recalled the sacrifices of the Old Covenant, in which "if the blood of goats and bulls... sanctifies in order to purification", he adds: "how much more will the blood of Christ, who by the Eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship to the living God."150 Even though we are aware of other possible interpretations, our consideration of the presence of the Holy Spirit throughout the entire life of Christ leads us to recognize this text as an invitation to also reflect on the presence of the same Spirit in the redemptive sacrifice of the Incarnate Word.

41. In the Old Testament we speak several times of the "fire from heaven", which burned the sacrifices presented by men.155 By analogy it can be said that the Holy Spirit is the "fire from heaven" that acts in the depths of the mystery of the Cross. Coming from the Father, it offers the Father the sacrifice of the Son, introducing him into the divine reality of Trinitarian communion. If sin has engendered suffering, now the pain of God in the crucified Christ receives its full human expression through the Holy Spirit. Thus a paradoxical mystery of love occurs: in Christ God suffers, rejected by his own creature: "They do not believe in me"; but, at the same time, from the depths of this suffering – and indirectly from the depths of the same sin “of not having believed” – the Spirit brings out a new dimension of the gift made to man and to creation from the beginning. In the depths of the mystery of the Cross, love acts, leading man again to participate in life, which is in God himself.

42. We have said that, at the culmination of the paschal mystery, the Holy Spirit is definitively revealed and made present in a new way. The risen Christ says to the apostles: "Receive the Holy Spirit." In this way the Holy Spirit is revealed, since the words of Christ constitute the confirmation of the promises and announcements of the discourse in the Cenacle. And with this the Paraclete is also made present in a new way. In reality, it was already acting from the beginning in the mystery of creation and throughout the entire history of the ancient Covenant of God with man. His action has been fully confirmed by the mission of the Son of Man as Messiah, who has come with the power of the Holy Spirit. At the culminating moment of Jesus' messianic mission, the Holy Spirit is present in the paschal mystery with all his divine subjectivity: as the one who must continue the saving work, based on the sacrifice of the Cross. Without a doubt this work is entrusted by Jesus to men: to the apostles and to the Church. However, in these men and through them, the Holy Spirit continues to be the transcendent protagonist of the realization of this work in the spirit of man and in the history of the world: the invisible and, at the same time, omnipresent Paraclete. The Spirit that "blows where it wills."159

43. The Second Vatican Council has recalled the Catholic teaching on conscience, when speaking of the vocation of man and, in particular, the dignity of the human person. Precisely conscience decides specifically about this dignity. In fact, conscience is "the most secret nucleus and the sanctuary of man", in which he feels alone with God, whose voice resonates in the most intimate space. This voice clearly says to "the ears of your heart warning you... do this, avoid that." Such ability to command good and prohibit evil, placed by the Creator in the heart of man, is the key property of the personal subject. But, at the same time, "in the depths of his conscience man discovers the existence of a law that he does not dictate to himself, but which he must obey."165 Conscience, therefore, is not an autonomous and exclusive source for deciding what is good or bad; On the contrary, a principle of obedience to the objective norm is deeply engraved in it, which grounds and conditions the congruence of its decisions with the precepts and prohibitions on which human behavior is based, as already glimpsed in the aforementioned page of the Book of Genesis.166 Precisely, in this sense, conscience is the "intimate tabernacle" where "the voice of God resounds." It is "the voice of God" even though man exclusively recognizes in it the principle of the moral order that cannot humanly be doubted, even without a direct reference to the Creator: precisely conscience always finds in this reference its foundation and its justification.

44. Well, in the Cenacle on the eve of his Passion, and then on the afternoon of Easter Day, Jesus Christ referred to the Holy Spirit as the one who testifies that sin persists in the history of humanity. However, sin is subject to the saving power of Redemption. "Convincing the world about sin" does not end with the fact that it is called by its name and identified for what it is in all its characteristic dimension. In convincing the world of sin, the Spirit of truth meets the voice of human consciences.

45. The Spirit of truth, who "convicts the world regarding sin", encounters that fatigue of human conscience, of which the conciliar texts speak in such a suggestive way. This fatigue of conscience also determines the paths of human conversions: turning one's back on sin to rebuild truth and love in the very heart of man. It is known that recognizing evil in oneself is often difficult. It is known that conscience not only commands or prohibits, but judges in the light of internal orders and prohibitions. It is also a source of remorse: man suffers internally for the evil committed. Is not this suffering like a distant echo of that "repentance for having created man", which with anthropomorphic language the sacred Book attributes to God; of that "reprobation" which, being inscribed in the "heart" of the Trinity, by virtue of eternal love is realized in the pain of the Cross and in the obedience of Christ until death? When the Spirit of truth allows the human conscience to participate in that pain, then the suffering of conscience is particularly profound and also salvific. For, through an act of perfect contrition, the authentic conversion of the heart is carried out: it is the evangelical "metanoia."

46. Within the framework of what has been said so far, other impressive and disconcerting words of Jesus are more understandable. We could call them the words of "non-forgiveness." The Synoptics refer them to us regarding a particular sin that is called "blasphemy against the Holy Spirit." This is how they have been referred to in their triple wording:

47. The action of the Spirit of truth, which tends to the saving "convince regarding sin", finds in the man who finds himself in this condition an internal resistance, like an impermeability of conscience, a state of mind that could be said to be consolidated by reason of a free choice: this is what Holy Scripture usually calls "hardness of heart".184 In our time, this attitude of mind and heart perhaps corresponds to the loss of the sense of sin, to which many pages are dedicated. Apostolic Exhortation Reconciliatio et paenitentia.185 Previously Pope Pius XII had stated that "the sin of our century is the loss of the sense of sin"186 and this loss is accompanied by the "loss of the sense of God." In the aforementioned Exhortation we read: «In reality, God is the root and supreme end of man and he carries within himself a divine germ. Therefore, it is the reality of God that discovers and illuminates the mystery of man. It is vain, therefore, to expect a consistent sense of sin with respect to man and human values, if the sense of the offense committed against God is lacking, that is, the true sense of sin. "187 The Church, therefore, does not cease to implore God for the grace that righteousness in human consciences is not diminished, that their healthy sensitivity to good and evil is not attenuated. This righteousness and sensitivity are deeply linked to the intimate action of the Spirit of truth. In this light, the Apostle's exhortations acquire a particular meaning: "Do not quench the Spirit," "do not grieve the Holy Spirit."188 But the Church, above all, does not cease to beg with great fervor that that sin called by the Gospel blasphemy against the Holy Spirit does not increase in the world; rather, it recedes in the souls of men and also in the same environments and in the different forms of society, giving rise to the opening of consciences, necessary for the saving action of the Holy Spirit. The Church prays that the dangerous sin against the Spirit gives way to a holy willingness to accept his mission as Paraclete, when he comes to "convince the world regarding sin, regarding justice and regarding judgment."

48. Jesus in his farewell speech has united these three areas of "convincing" as components of the mission of the Paraclete: sin, justice and judgment. They point out the dimension of that mystery of piety, which in the history of man is opposed to sin, that is, to the mystery of impiety.189 On the one hand, as Saint Augustine expresses himself, there is "love of oneself to the point of contempt for God"; on the other, there is the "love of God to the point of self-contempt."190 The Church constantly raises her prayer and exercises her ministry so that the history of consciences and the history of societies in the great human family do not descend to the pole of sin with the rejection of God's commandments "to the point of contempt for God," but, on the contrary, rise toward the love in which the Spirit who gives life is manifested.

49. The thoughts and hearts of the Church turn to the Holy Spirit at the end of the twentieth century and in the perspective of the third millennium of the coming of Jesus Christ to the world, as we look to the great Jubilee with which the Church will celebrate this event. In effect, this coming is measured, according to the calculation of time, as an event that belongs to the history of man on earth. The commonly used measurement of time determines years, centuries and millennia depending on whether they occur before or after the birth of Christ. But we must also keep in mind that, for us Christians, this event means, according to the Apostle, the "fullness of time,"193 because through them God himself, with his "measure," completely penetrated the history of man: he is a transcendent presence in the eternal "now" ([+[0]+]). «He who is, who was and who is to come»; he who is "the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End."194 "For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life."195 "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman... so that we might receive sonship."196 and this incarnation of the Word-Son took place "by the work of the Holy Spirit ».

50. The great Jubilee, which will conclude the second millennium for which the Church is already preparing, directly has a Christological dimension; Indeed, it is about celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ. At the same time, it has a pneumatological dimension, since the mystery of the Incarnation was carried out "by the work of the Holy Spirit." It was "performed by that Spirit who, "consubstantial with the Father and the Son," is, in the absolute mystery of the triune God, the Person-love, the uncreated gift, the eternal source of every gift that comes from God in the order of creation, the direct principle and, in a certain way, the subject of God's self-communication in the order of grace. The mystery of the Incarnation of God constitutes the culmination of this gift and this divine self-communication.

51. All this is carried out by the work of the Holy Spirit and, consequently, belongs to the content of the future great Jubilee. The Church cannot prepare for this in any other way, except through the Holy Spirit. What was accomplished in "the fullness of time" by the work of the Holy Spirit can only now emerge from the memory of the Church by his work. Through his work he can be present in the new phase of the history of man on earth: the two thousandth year of the birth of Christ.

52. The work of the Spirit "who gives life" reaches its culmination in the mystery of the Incarnation. It is not possible to give life, which is fully in God, without making it the life of a Man, as Christ is in his humanity personalized by the Word in the hypostatic union. And at the same time, with the mystery of the Incarnation, the source of this divine life in the history of humanity is opened in a new way: the Holy Spirit. THE Word, "Firstborn of all creation", becomes "the firstborn among many brothers"210 and thus also becomes the head of the body that is the Church, which will be born on the Cross and will be revealed on the day of Pentecost; and in the Church he is the head of humanity: of men of every nation, race, region and culture, language and continent, who have been called to salvation. « The Word became flesh; ( [+[0]+] ) there was life, and life was the Light of men... To all who received it he gave power to become children of God. "211 But all this was carried out and continues to be carried out incessantly "by the work of the Holy Spirit."

53. It can be said that all this falls within the scope of the great Jubilee mentioned above. In fact, it is necessary to go beyond the historical dimension of the fact, considered externally. It is necessary to insert, in the same Christological content of the event, the pneumatological dimension, encompassing with the gaze of faith the two millennia of the action of the Spirit of truth, which, through the centuries, has received from the treasure of the Redemption of Christ, giving men new life, carrying out adoption in them in the only begotten Son, sanctifying them, in such a way that they can repeat with Saint Paul: "we have received the Spirit that comes from God."221 But continuing with the theme of the Jubilee, it is not possible to limit ourselves to the two thousand years that have passed since the birth of Christ. We must look back, understand all the action of the Holy Spirit even before Christ: from the beginning, throughout the world and, especially, in the economy of the Old Alliance. In fact, this action in every place and time, even more so, in each man, has been developed according to the eternal plan of salvation, by which it is intimately linked to the mystery of the Incarnation and Redemption, which in turn exerted its influence on believers in Christ who was to come. This is particularly attested to by the Letter to the Ephesians.222 Therefore, grace carries with it a Christological and at the same time pneumatological characteristic that is verified above all in those who explicitly adhere to Christ: "In him ([+[0]+]) ... you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of Promise, which is a pledge of our inheritance for the redemption of the People of its possession."223

54. "God is spirit, and those who worship must worship in spirit and truth." 226 These words were spoken by Jesus in another of his conversations: that one with the Samaritan woman. The great Jubilee, which will be celebrated at the end of this millennium and the beginning of the next, must constitute a strong call addressed to all those who "worship God in spirit and truth." It should be a special occasion for everyone to meditate on the mystery of the triune God, who in himself is completely transcendent with respect to the world, especially the visible world. In effect, it is absolute Spirit: "God is spirit"; 227 and at the same time, and in an admirable way, it is not only close to this world, but it is present in it and, in a certain way, immanent, it penetrates and vivifies it from within. This is especially true for man: God is in the depths of his being as thought, conscience, heart; It is a psychological and ontological reality to which Saint Augustine said: "it is more intimate than my intimacy."228 These words help us to better understand those that Jesus addressed to the Samaritan woman: "God is spirit." Only the Spirit can be “closer to my intimacy” both in being and in spiritual experience; Only the Spirit can be so immanent to man and the world, remaining inviolable and immutable in its absolute transcendence.

55. Unfortunately, throughout the history of salvation it turns out that the closeness and presence of God in man and in the world, that admirable condescension of the Spirit, encounters resistance and opposition in our human reality. From this point of view, the prophetic words of the old Simeon are very eloquent, who "moved by the Spirit, came to the Temple of Jerusalem to announce to the newborn of Bethlehem that he "is destined for the fall and rise of many in Israel, and to be a sign of contradiction."232 The opposition to God, who is an invisible Spirit, is already born in a certain way on the ground of the radical diversity of the world with respect to him, that is, of his "visibility" and "materiality" in relation to he, "invisible" and "absolute" Spirit; It is born from its essential and inevitable imperfection with respect to it, being most perfect. But the opposition becomes drama and rebellion in the ethical field, due to that sin that takes possession of the human heart, in which "the flesh has desires contrary to the spirit, and the spirit contrary to the flesh."233 As we have already said, the Spirit must "convince the world" regarding this sin.

56. Unfortunately, resistance to the Holy Spirit, which Saint Paul emphasizes in the interior and subjective dimension as tension, struggle and rebellion that takes place in the human heart, finds in different historical periods and, especially, in the modern era, its external dimension, concentrating as the content of culture and civilization, as a philosophical system, as an ideology, as a program of action and formation of human behavior. It finds its maximum expression in materialism, either in its theoretical form - as a system of thought - or in its practical form - as a method of reading and evaluating facts - and also as a corresponding behavioral program. The system that has given maximum development and has taken this form of thought, ideology and praxis to its extreme practical consequences is dialectical and historical materialism, recognized today as the vital core of Marxism.

57. In the Pauline contrast between the "spirit" and the "flesh" the contrast between "life" and "death" is also included. This is a serious problem about which it must now be said that materialism, as a system of thought in any of its versions, means the acceptance of death as the definitive end of human existence. Everything that is material is corruptible and, therefore, the human body ( [+[0]+] ) is mortal. If man in his essence is only "flesh", death is for him a border and an insurmountable term. Then it is understood that it can be said that human life is exclusively an "existing to die."

58. The mystery of the Resurrection and Pentecost is announced and lived by the Church, which is the heir and continuer of the testimony of the Apostles about the resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is the perennial witness of the victory over death, which revealed the strength of the Holy Spirit and determined its new coming, its new presence in men and in the world. Indeed, in the resurrection of Christ, the Holy Spirit Paraclete revealed himself above all as the one who gives life: "He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you."247 In the name of the resurrection of Christ the Church announces the life, which has manifested itself beyond the limit of death, the life that is stronger than death. At the same time, he announces the one who gives life: the life-giving Spirit; He announces it and cooperates with him in giving life. Indeed, "although the body has already died because of sin, the spirit is life because of justice" 248 accomplished by the crucified and resurrected Christ. And in the name of the resurrection of Christ, the Church serves the life that comes from God himself, in intimate union and humble service to the Spirit. Precisely through this service man becomes in an ever new way "the way of the Church", as I already said in the Encyclical on Christ the Redeemer 249 and now I repeat in this one on the Holy Spirit. The Church, united to the Spirit, is aware more than anyone else of the reality of the inner man, of what is most profound and essential in man, because he is spiritual and incorruptible. At this level the Spirit grafts the "root of immortality",250 from which new life springs, that is, the life of man in God which, as a fruit of his saving communication by the Holy Spirit, can develop and consolidate only under his action. For this reason, the Apostle addresses God on behalf of believers, to whom he says: "I bow my knees before the Father... so that he may grant you that you may be strengthened by the action of his Spirit in the inner man."251

59. The intimate relationship with God through the Holy Spirit makes man understand, in a new way, also himself and his own humanity. In this way, that image and likeness of God that is man from the beginning is fully realized.255 This intimate truth about the human being must be constantly discovered in the light of Christ who is the prototype of the relationship with God and, in him, the reason for "the sincere giving of oneself to others" must also be discovered, as the Second Vatican Council writes; Precisely because of this divine resemblance, it is demonstrated that man "is the only terrestrial creature whom God has loved for himself," in his dignity as a person, but open to integration and social communion.256 Effective knowledge and full realization of this truth of being are given only by the work of the Holy Spirit. Man comes to know this truth through Jesus Christ and puts it into practice in his life through the work of the Spirit, which Jesus himself has given us.

60. When, under the influence of the Paraclete, men discover this divine dimension of their being and their life, either as individuals or as a community, they are capable of freeing themselves from the various determinisms derived mainly from the materialist bases of thought, praxis and their respective methodology. In our time these factors have managed to penetrate to the most intimate part of man, into the sanctuary of conscience, where the Holy Spirit constantly infuses the light and strength of new life according to the freedom of the children of God. Man's maturity in this life is impeded by the conditions and pressures exerted on him by the dominant structures and mechanisms in the various sectors of society. It can be said that in many cases social factors, instead of favoring the development and expansion of the human spirit, end up tearing it away from the genuine truth of its being and its life, "over which the Holy Spirit watches over" in order to subject it to the "Prince of this world."

61. Approaching the end of the second millennium, which must remind everyone and almost make present again of the coming of the Word in the fullness of time, the Church, once again, tries to penetrate into the very essence of its divine-human constitution and of that mission that makes it participate in the messianic mission of Christ, according to the teaching and always valid plan of the Second Vatican Council. Following this line, we can go back to the Cenacle where Jesus Christ reveals the Holy Spirit as Paraclete, as Spirit of truth, and speaks of his own "departure" through the Cross as a necessary condition of his "coming": "It is to your advantage that I depart; because if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send it to you. "267 We have seen that this announcement has already had its first realization on the afternoon of Easter Day and then during the celebration of Pentecost in Jerusalem, and that since then it has been verified in the history of humanity through the Church.

62. The most complete sacramental expression of the departure of Christ through the mystery of the Cross and the Resurrection is the Eucharist. In it his coming and his saving presence are carried out sacramentally each time: in the Sacrifice and in Communion. It is carried out by the work of the Holy Spirit, within his own mission.270 Through the Eucharist the Holy Spirit carries out that "strengthening of the inner man" of which the Letter to the Ephesians speaks.271 Through the Eucharist, people and communities, under the action of the comforting Paraclete, learn to discover the divine meaning of human life, alluded to by the Council: the sense by which Jesus Christ "fully reveals man to man", suggesting "a certain similarity between the union of the divine Persons and the union of the children of God in truth and charity. "272 This union is expressed and realized especially through the Eucharist in which man, participating in the sacrifice of Christ, which such a celebration actualizes, also learns to "find himself... in the sincere gift of himself"273 in communion with God and with other men, his brothers.

63. The Eucharistic presence of Christ, his sacramental "I am with you", allows the Church to discover more and more deeply its own mystery, as attested by the entire ecclesiology of the Second Vatican Council, for which "the Church is in Christ a sacrament, that is, a sign or instrument of the intimate union with God and of the unity of the entire human race."277 As a sacrament, the Church develops from the paschal mystery of the "departure" of Christ, living from his " always new coming by the work of the Holy Spirit, within the same mission of the Paraclete-Spirit of truth. This is precisely the essential mystery of the Church as the Council proclaims.

64. If the Church is the sacrament of intimate union with God, it is in Jesus Christ, in whom this same union is verified as a saving reality. It is in Jesus Christ, by the work of the Holy Spirit. The fullness of the saving reality, which is Christ in history, is spread sacramentally by the power of the Paraclete Spirit. In this way, the Holy Spirit is "the other Paraclete" or "new consoler" because, through his action, the Good News takes shape in human consciences and hearts and spreads throughout history. In everything there is the Holy Spirit who gives life.

65. The breath of divine life, the Holy Spirit, in its simplest and most common way, manifests and makes itself felt in prayer. It is beautiful and healthy to think that, wherever you pray in the world, there is the Holy Spirit, the vital breath of prayer. It is beautiful and healthy to recognize that if prayer is spread throughout the world, in the past, in the present and in the future, the presence and action of the Holy Spirit is equally widespread, which "encourages" prayer in the heart of man in the entire immense range of the most diverse situations and conditions, whether favorable or adverse to spiritual and religious life. Many times, under the action of the Spirit, prayer springs from the heart of man despite prohibitions and persecutions, and even official proclamations about the non-religious or even atheistic nature of public life. Prayer is always the voice of all those who apparently have no voice, and in this voice always resounds that "mighty cry", which the Letter to the Hebrews attributes to Christ.280 Prayer is also the revelation of that abyss that is the heart of man: a depth that belongs to God and that only God can fill, precisely with the Holy Spirit. We read in Saint Luke: "If you, then, being evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him."281

66. In the midst of the problems, disappointments and hopes, desertions and returns of our time, the Church remains faithful to the mystery of its birth. If it is a historical fact that the Church left the Cenacle on the day of Pentecost, it can be said in a certain way that it has never left it. Spiritually, the event of Pentecost does not belong only to the past: the Church is always in the Cenacle that she carries in her heart. The Church perseveres in prayer, like the Apostles with Mary, Mother of Christ, and with those who constituted the first germ of the Christian community in Jerusalem and awaited, in prayer, the coming of the Holy Spirit.

67. We wish to conclude these considerations in the heart of the Church and in the heart of man. The path of the Church passes through the heart of man because here is the hidden place of the saving encounter with the Holy Spirit, with the hidden God and, precisely here, the Holy Spirit becomes a "fountain of water springing up to eternal life."289 He arrives here as the Spirit of truth and as a Paraclete, in the same way as had been promised by Christ. From here he acts as Comforter, Intercessor and Advocate, especially when man, or humanity, finds himself before the judgment of condemnation of that "accuser", who the Apocalypse says "accuses" our brothers day and night before our God".290 The Holy Spirit does not cease to be the custodian of hope in the heart of man: the hope of all human creatures and, especially, of those who "possess the firstfruits of the Spirit" and "await redemption." of his body".291
